SAM 3 · ICLR 2026

SAM 3 and the Problem of Finding Every Match

SAM 3 turns a short concept prompt into masks for matching objects across images and video. Its most revealing test may be a prompt whose answer should be empty.

THE SHORT VERSION

  • Finding every match requires testing absent concepts as well as visible ones.
  • Short concept phrases are not unrestricted visual reasoning.
  • Report first-pass errors and the human effort required to repair them.
01 / CLOSER READING

The problem: every match includes the possibility of none

Ask a visual tool to find red cups on a crowded desk. A striking demonstration might highlight one obvious cup. A dependable tool needs a stricter contract: include every matching instance, exclude the red stapler, and return nothing when no cup matches. In video, it should also keep the same cup's identity as objects move. These are different obligations. A system can draw excellent boundaries while missing objects, or find the right set while switching identities. SAM 3 makes this broader contract central to the interface between language and pixels.

02 / CLOSER READING

Mechanism: separate concept recognition from tracking

The original SAM 3 paper defines promptable concept segmentation around short noun phrases or visual exemplars. A detector locates matching instances, while a memory-based tracker follows them through video. They share a visual encoder but serve different purposes: detection finds the category's members; tracking distinguishes individuals over time. A separate presence head helps decide whether the requested concept exists, rather than forcing localization to carry the entire recognition problem.

Training includes difficult negative phrases. The authors' ablations attribute gains to both those negatives and the presence mechanism. The paper also evaluates an optional higher-level agent that uses SAM 3 as a tool. That distinction matters: the base model's short-phrase task is not the same capability as an additional language model interpreting a complicated request.

03 / CLOSER READING

Actual evidence: the benchmark tests an image–prompt pair

Meta's SA-Co/Gold documentation treats an image and its noun phrase as the evaluation unit. A phrase may have several annotated objects or no matching object. Independent annotations can disagree about boundaries, instance counts, or whether the concept is present. The official evaluator compares predictions against the available annotations using a specified matching procedure. This makes annotation policy part of the result, not a detail to ignore when comparing systems.

The public repository provides inference examples, model checkpoints, and evaluation resources. Its image interface returns masks, boxes, and scores; video examples include interactive refinement. These are useful ingredients for reproduction, but a released notebook is not evidence that every downstream use will be reliable. We would inspect the evaluation configuration and save the exact model version before treating a reproduced number as comparable to the paper.

04 / CLOSER READING

Limitations: short phrases are a deliberate boundary

SAM 3's base formulation does not support unrestricted referring expressions or arbitrarily complex multi-attribute instructions. The original paper also notes that video inference cost increases with the number of tracked objects. Our report concerns that original SAM 3 system; the live repository now also contains SAM 3.1 updates, whose claims should not be silently substituted for the earlier results.

The dataset documentation adds a subtler limitation: 'all instances' depends on what can be separated and agreed upon. A crowded group may be annotated differently from clearly isolated objects. In our view, this is not a reason to dismiss the benchmark. It is a reason to understand the contract before building on it. An application that counts individual items may care about a distinction that a union-of-pixels evaluation does not fully capture.

05 / CLOSER READING

Our analysis: build a failure map before a showcase

For a student project, we would start with a small, deliberately awkward test collection rather than a highlight reel. Include an absent target, a visually similar distractor, several overlapping matches, a partly hidden object, and an object that leaves and re-enters the frame. Decide what the correct answer is before looking at model output. Where a phrase is genuinely ambiguous, record alternative acceptable interpretations instead of pretending there is one obvious answer.

Then score failures separately. Missed instances tell us about coverage. Incorrect inclusions tell us about selectivity. Boundary errors tell us about spatial precision. Identity switches tell us about temporal consistency. A single attractive overlay can conceal all four. The relative importance should follow the application: an editing assistant may tolerate a quick manual correction, while a counting pipeline may propagate one missed object into every later calculation.

We would also measure the cost of repair. If a user can correct a mask with an example or point, does that correction apply to the intended instance without changing unrelated objects? Does it persist across frames? Recording the first prediction and every subsequent intervention prevents an interactive success from being mistaken for autonomous performance. That is a test protocol we propose, not a result reported by SAM 3.

06 / CLOSER READING

Takeaway: an empty answer can be the right answer

SAM 3 is useful to think with because it makes language-conditioned selection more explicit. The engineering opportunity is not merely to produce pleasing masks; it is to expose a selection contract that can be checked and repaired. Before asking how impressive the demo looks, ask which failure your application cannot afford—and whether your evaluation includes enough opportunities for that failure to appear. Sometimes the strongest evidence of understanding is a system that correctly selects nothing.
